positive: Many Samsung Fold owners say they are happy with their devices and welcome Apple into the foldable space, with some admitting they are impressed.
Several commenters note Samsung has offered foldables for years, and hope the added competition pushes it to improve.
Apple's pencil support is seen as a weak spot for Samsung, with some wanting stylus support and water resistance back and calling the Duo appealing.
negative: Many commenters say Apple's foldable arrives years after Samsung's and copies its ideas, so it doesn't feel like a true first-generation product.
Some criticize Samsung's foldables for durability and software problems, such as screens failing after about a year, slowdowns over time, and trade-offs in thinness and features.
Others question the new device's size, weight and price, calling it too small or heavy and too expensive.

positive: Many viewers are impressed that the crease is barely visible or not noticeable, and see the matte inner screen as a smart way to hide it.
The matte finish and overall look of the inner display are praised as attractive and a thoughtful touch.
negative: Many dislike the matte, nano-texture-style inner screen, saying it looks washed out, grainy or inaccurate in color and lacks a glossy OLED look.
Commenters see the matte finish as a way to hide the crease, and say Apple doesn't show off the hinge or crease.
Several worry the inner display is fragile, with concerns about scratches when left open and about durability of repeated folding.

positive: Many commenters say the open and close animation is smooth, clean and polished, and that the designers deserve recognition or a reward.
Several Samsung fans and Apple skeptics concede the animation is impressive, and some say it is the most appealing part of the phone.
The effect of the front panel looking see-through, and animations that follow the hinge angle, drew praise, with one noting the possibilities for app developers.
negative: Many commenters say the price is far too high, especially with everyday costs rising, and that it is higher still in several other countries.
Several mock the folding animation as the headline feature, saying it is underwhelming for a flagship after so many years of development.
Some worry about durability and repair costs, and say competitors like Samsung offer better value through discounts.

positive: Many commenters plan to swap a Pro model for the Duo, saying they are excited by a new form factor after years of similar phones.
Viewers value a larger screen that folds to a pocketable size, expecting to carry an iPad or laptop less often.
Several say the camera and other Pro-level compromises matter little for everyday use, and note the Duo was never pitched as a Pro.
negative: Many commenters see the Duo's price as too high, especially when it comes with trade-offs compared with a Pro or Pro Max.
Camera downgrades and the missing Face ID are the most common deal breakers, with several choosing the 18 Pro or Pro Max.
Some call the Duo unproven or not ready, and plan to wait for a later version or keep their current phone.

positive: Several left-handed commenters say they would adapt to the device and still want it, treating handedness as a minor concern.
Commenters like the button and toolbar placement. They say it suits tablet-style use, pocket access and one-handed screenshots, and they don't mind it for left-handed use.
Many viewers praise the size and half-folded shape, and see uses for reading, medical work, navigation and retro-style gaming.
negative: Left-handed users expect the design to suit them poorly, with several commenters saying the layout seems built only for right-handed people.
The phone's weight, width when folded and added case thickness are seen as making one-handed use awkward or uncomfortable.
Some note that the unfolded layout puts key elements, such as the text field, awkwardly near the hinge.

positive: Many commenters say they are ready to buy, drawn by a foldable that works as both phone and tablet, replacing an aging iPad mini.
Several accept trade-offs like no telephoto camera or Touch ID, saying the screen, software and polished fold animation matter more.
Some plan to add extra protection such as AppleCare or pick larger storage, while one points to a cheaper rival with stronger specs.
negative: Many commenters see the price, around the $2,000+ range and far higher for top storage, as unaffordable, with jokes about loans and financing.
The price is seen as too high for what is offered, such as a missing Pro-level camera and design they consider basic or not new.
Some doubt demand or practical value, citing durability worries, awkward half-folded use, and not wanting a costly device that encourages more phone time.

positive: Many commenters say they are eager to buy the Duo, with some planning to pre-order and others saying they have waited a long time for a foldable iPhone.
Several see it as the first genuinely interesting iPhone in years, praising its design, premium materials, polished open/close feel and the ability to multitask.
Some note that foldable features already existed on Android, but even Android users and sceptics say they admire it or are being won over.
negative: Many commenters see the Duo as too expensive and plan to wait for a later generation, expecting first-gen flaws and a lighter, improved design.
Commenters doubt Apple's innovation, saying it holds back features for next year, copies rivals, and has let its iPhone design go stale.
Some worry about the durability of a first-generation foldable screen, and others question whether a foldable is useful or just a gimmick.

positive: Many commenters say Apple's software and UI feel polished and fluid, and that this sets the device apart from rivals.
Several people say idea-sharing between tech companies benefits consumers, and that competitors tend to follow whatever Apple does.
Many longtime Apple users express strong excitement and plan to buy it, citing the design, build quality and trust in the brand.
negative: Many commenters say Apple is borrowing features Android makers, especially Samsung, have offered for years, such as foldables, and call it unoriginal.
Some say the criticism should extend to other companies that follow trends rather than standing apart, not just Apple.
Others focus on the high price, first-generation risk, missing features and App Store restrictions, and say they will wait for later models.
Many commenters say the price is too high, and import costs make it even worse in some countries, such as Turkey, Australia and Bolivia.
Storage upgrades are seen as costly, and the base capacity is considered small for the price. Some note it costs more than an iPad.
Some doubt the value and build: basic software like autocorrect still seems flawed, the device may be awkward to open, and an older used iPad looks like a better buy.
